analysis.one_liner: Lets people crushed by medical bills keep more assets and erase more debts in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: A bill to ease bankruptcy rules for people with large medical bills was introduced in the Senate's final weeks and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new category of "medically distressed debtor" — someone whose unpaid medical bills over three years topped the lesser of 10% of their income or $10,000, or who lost work because of illness or caregiving. Those debtors could skip the bankruptcy means test and credit counseling, keep up to $250,000 in home value, and wipe out student loans like other debts. It died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Families whose finances were wrecked by medical bills — including people who went broke caring for a sick relative, missed work due to illness, or were hit by COVID-era job loss. In bankruptcy, they could keep more home equity, avoid means-test hurdles that can force them into a longer repayment plan, and discharge student loans alongside medical debt.

how_it_helps.text: Medically distressed debtors would be exempt from the bankruptcy means test, which otherwise can block a Chapter 7 filing or push a filer into a multi-year repayment plan.
They could exempt up to $250,000 in home equity or other residential property, above what federal or state law would otherwise allow.
They could skip the pre-filing credit counseling requirement.
Their student loans would be dischargeable in bankruptcy without proving 'undue hardship,' which is normally a very high bar.
Eligibility covers medical bills for the debtor, dependents, and close relatives, and covers people who lost wages or jobs because of illness, caregiving, or a declared public health emergency.

analysis.who_pays: Creditors who are owed money by medical debtors — hospitals and other medical providers, credit card issuers and lenders holding unpaid medical bills, and debt collectors — would recover less in bankruptcy, and some of that cost can be spread through higher prices or tighter lending to other customers.

drawbacks.text: The bill waives the means test entirely for medically distressed debtors, so a filer with substantial income who crosses the medical-debt threshold could erase debts that the 2005 bankruptcy law was designed to make them repay; the only anti-abuse safeguard is a signed statement, under penalty of perjury, that medical expenses were not run up to qualify.

Creditors — including hospitals and community lenders — would recover less from these bankruptcies, and creditors typically recoup such losses through pricing and lending terms charged to everyone else.
The $250,000 home-equity exemption is uniform nationwide and would let some debtors shield significant assets that current law exposes in many states.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are targeted at a real and well-documented hardship — medical bills are a leading driver of personal bankruptcy — and the eligibility tests (bills above 10% of income or $10,000, or illness-driven job loss) aim the relief at people genuinely in distress. The trade-offs are real: the means-test waiver and the large flat home-equity exemption would let some better-off filers escape repayment obligations, and creditors' losses get spread into prices and lending terms. On balance the bill's benefits concentrate on the families it names, while its costs are diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last weeks of the two-year Congress and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never considered it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on November 21, 2024, with five Democratic colleagues joining as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Creditors with claims against medical debtors — hospitals, card issuers, lenders, and collectors — keep the full collection rights they would have lost under the bill. Bankruptcy rules stay exactly as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Creditors, who kept existing collection rights

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medical Bankruptcy Fairness Act and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, Peter Welch, Martin Heinrich (Luján), Tammy Baldwin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill's support never extended beyond these six Democrats.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin, D-IL, in the 118th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate majority at the time of introduction (Republicans held 49 seats; Democrats controlled the chamber through the lame-duck session)
against.what_they_did: The bill had no Republican cosponsors and no floor action occurred before the Congress ended; with no committee progress, leadership never faced a request to schedule it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and it never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: Unpaid medical bills are what pushes these debtors into bankruptcy; the bill would make more of that debt dischargeable and let debtors keep home equity that could otherwise be liquidated to pay providers. Providers could recoup through pricing, which spreads the cost to other patients.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: Medical bills are often carried on credit cards and personal loans; easier Chapter 7 relief and a waived means test mean these creditors collect less. Costs get passed on through interest rates and lending terms.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and medical debt buyers
industries.note: Their business is buying and collecting unpaid medical debt; broader discharge protections reduce the value of what they collect.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and the federal student loan portfolio
industries.note: The bill would let medically distressed debtors discharge student loans without the 'undue hardship' showing, though only for debtors who meet the medical-debt threshold.
